strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored question in equivariant learning: whether the implicit assumption that transformed samples are equally likely under the test distribution actually holds in practice, and how its violation affects equivariant methods.

The proposed metric m(p_X) via a classifier two-sample test is simple, interpretable, practical, and validated thoughtfully: sanity checks on rotated/canonicalized datasets, ablations on classifier architecture (Table 6 shows robustness for the task-independent metric), p-value computations, and comparisons against MMD variants with different point-cloud kernels.

The theoretical contribution is substantive: Theorems 1-3 give a careful analysis of ridge(less) regression under non-symmetric covariance, showing test-time symmetrization can blow up risk while data augmentation remains helpful in the under-parameterized regime, and can be harmful in the over-parameterized regime via correlations between invariant and non-invariant features. The deterministic-equivalent derivations (Appendix A.6) are technically solid, and the authors are admirably honest that the calculational machinery follows prior work, with the novelty being the application to invariant learning.

Empirical findings are interesting and wide-ranging: most benchmark point-cloud datasets (QM9, ModelNet40, rMD17, OC20, LLM materials data) are highly canonicalized; augmentation helps on molecular datasets despite canonicalization but hurts on MNIST/ModelNet40; the local-vs-global analysis (local QM9, local ModelNet40) provides a plausible mechanistic explanation tying canonicalization findings to the known success of locally equivariant methods.

Strong reproducibility: extensive experimental details (models, hyperparameters, training times, hardware), a supplemental codebase with a README, and thorough appendices (70 pages) covering theory proofs, metric derivations, and per-dataset experiment details.

The paper is clearly written, honestly reports negative/inconclusive results (e.g., task-dependent metric being architecture-sensitive and inconclusive on real datasets), and carefully positions itself against related work (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy, Elesedy & Zaidi, Wang et al.).
weaknesses: The core methodology is a fairly direct application of classifier two-sample tests (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2017) to the specific question of distributional symmetry breaking; the methodological novelty relative to Chiu & Bloem-Reddy (2023) is mainly replacing MMD/kernel choice with classifier accuracy, which is a sensible but incremental design decision.

The paper is largely diagnostic/descriptive rather than prescriptive: despite the title framing ('To Augment or Not to Augment?'), no actionable rule emerges for deciding when augmentation will help. The central empirical surprise (augmentation still helps on canonicalized QM9/QM7b but hurts on MNIST/ModelNet40) remains unexplained beyond the locality hypothesis, which the authors themselves admit is correlational ('challenging to establish a causal link').

The task-dependent metric is weak as a practical tool: it is highly sensitive to the choice of canonicalization and classifier architectures (Tables 2 and 3 show accuracies ranging from ~52% to ~89% under small architecture changes), and it is inconclusive on the real datasets it is most needed for, leaving the most interesting prediction question open.

The theory is confined to linear/ridge regression; while the NTK connection is invoked, the gap between the linear analysis and the deep-network experiments (transformers, equivariant GNNs) is not bridged, so the theory does not quantitatively predict the empirical outcomes.

Experimental baselines are not state-of-the-art (e.g., older Graphormer and small e3nn models on QM9), which is justified for controlled comparisons but weakens the practical significance of the augmentation findings for the community; some results (e.g., FT catastrophic failures at 16-40% accuracy) are dominated by obvious distribution shift.

Some parts read as a collection of case studies rather than a unified conclusion: findings vary per dataset, per molecule (rMD17), and per property (QM9), and the paper's takeaways are appropriately hedged but leave the significance of the metric for practitioners somewhat diffuse.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting and underexplored question: whether data distributions actually satisfy the implicit symmetry (isotropy) assumptions underlying equivariant methods and data augmentation. The distinction between distributional and functional symmetry breaking is clearly articulated.

The proposed classifier two-sample test metric m(pX) is simple, interpretable, and easy to implement, and the authors carefully position it against the MMD-based tests of Chiu & Bloem-Reddy (2023), avoiding the kernel-selection problem. Finite-group analysis (optimal accuracy interpolation) adds interpretability.

The theoretical analysis of ridge(less) regression under non-symmetric covariance is nontrivial: Theorems 1-3 characterize when test-time symmetrization and data augmentation can hurt even with invariant ground truth, including a blow-up at the interpolation threshold. The deterministic-equivalent derivations (Appendix A.6-A.7) are solid and empirically validated (Figure 6).

The empirical survey is broad: MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM crystal-generation dataset. Useful secondary analyses (local vs. global QM9, moments of inertia, per-class ModelNet40 breakdown, interpretability of the classifier, architecture ablations) support the locality hypothesis for why equivariance helps on canonicalized data.

The paper is honest about negative results (e.g., train-time augmentation still helps on QM9/QM7b despite high canonicalization; task-dependent metric is inconclusive on real datasets), and includes a large appendix with training details, p-values, and reproduction instructions.
weaknesses: The central practical question implied by the title ('To Augment or Not to Augment?') is ultimately not answered. The paper's own results show that high distributional symmetry breaking does NOT consistently predict when augmentation hurts (augmentation helps on highly canonicalized QM9/QM7b but hurts on canonicalized MNIST/ModelNet40), and the proposed task-dependent metric is admitted to be inconclusive on real datasets. Thus the diagnostic tool has limited demonstrated predictive utility.

The metric itself is not a rigorous measure of 'degree' of symmetry breaking: classifier accuracy depends on architecture, training, sample size, and group cardinality, and m(pX) near 1 does not distinguish 'canonicalized' from other sparse-support scenarios (footnote 4 concedes this). The claim that it is a 'metric' overstates what a single classifier's held-out accuracy provides.

Limited technical novelty in the metric: applying classifier two-sample tests (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2017) to compare a distribution against its group-symmetrized version is a fairly direct combination of existing tools, and prior work (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy, 2023; Desai et al., 2022; Urbano & Romero, 2024) already covers closely related ground. The incremental contribution is primarily application and packaging.

The theory is confined to linear/ridge regression with Gaussian data and a specific minimal covariance model. The connection from these results to the deep learning experiments (Graphormer, e3nn, CNNs) is loose and largely analogical; no theory explains the most surprising empirical finding (augmentation helping on canonicalized QM9).

Experimental comparisons have confounds: the non-equivariant models use absolute-position embeddings while the equivariant baselines differ substantially in architecture and training details; some reported numbers (e.g., FF on MNIST 98.89% vs. equivariant 97.8%) raise questions about whether 'FF benefits' are simply standard generalization effects of augmentation rather than symmetry-specific phenomena. Ablations isolating these confounds are incomplete.

Significance is moderated by the mixed conclusions: the actionable takeaway for practitioners is thin, and the most interesting hypotheses (locality, task-useful symmetry breaking) are explicitly deferred to future work. The paper reads more as an empirical study/diagnostic proposal than as a contribution with clear, supported prescriptions.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely interesting and underexplored question: when does the implicit assumption that p(x) ≈ p(gx) underlying equivariant methods actually hold in practice? This is a natural and important follow-up to Elesedy & Zaidi (2021) and Wang et al. (2023, 2024d).

The proposed classifier two-sample test metric m(pX) is simple, interpretable, practical, and well-motivated relative to kernel-based alternatives (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy, 2023), avoiding kernel selection issues; the finite-group analysis (Section 2) providing the optimal-accuracy calculation 1 − (1/2)Σ min(1/r, θi) is a nice touch.

Extensive empirical validation across many datasets (MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, LLM crystal data) with sanity checks (rotated/canonicalized controls, augmented-fraction sweeps), per-class analyses, and robustness ablations showing insensitivity to classifier architecture (Table 6).

The theoretical contribution is substantive: generalizing Elesedy & Zaidi (2021, Theorem 7) to non-invariant data, showing augmentation always helps in the under-parameterized ridgeless regime but can hurt in the over-parameterized regime when invariant and non-invariant features are correlated (Theorem 3), with deterministic-equivalent derivations via random matrix theory and simulation confirmation (Figure 6).

The locality experiments (Section 5.3, Appendix C.6) provide a plausible mechanistic explanation for why equivariance/augmentation still helps on canonicalized datasets like QM9, and the distinction between detection accuracy and true canonicalization (predicting g from gx, Table 8) is thoughtful.
The paper is honest about limitations (e.g., task-dependent metric being inconclusive/sensitive to architecture) and provides extensive appendices, training details, and a reproduction codebase.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest: the core metric is a direct application of the classifier two-sample test of Lopez-Paz & Oquab (2017) to the symmetrized-vs-original comparison; the empirical findings (e.g., ModelNet40 pre-alignment, CORINA canonicalization of QM9 conformers) are partially known or expected from prior work, so the surprise factor is somewhat diluted.

The theory is restricted to linear ridge regression with Gaussian data; the link to neural networks via NTK-style reasoning is only heuristic, and it is unclear how the over-parameterized risk-blowup phenomena map onto the deep networks used in the experiments.

The central empirical puzzle—why train-time augmentation helps on highly canonicalized QM9/QM7b—remains unresolved; the locality hypothesis is only correlational ('challenging to establish a causal link') and the paper offers no predictive rule for when to augment.

The task-dependent metric (Section 5.2, Appendix B) is largely inconclusive: it fails on MNIST, is 'overly sensitive to the canonicalization and classifier network architectures' (Tables 2 and 3 show accuracy varying from ~68% to ~89% with architecture), and does not predict augmentation benefit on QM7b. This limits the practical value of the metric framework.

Equivariant baselines are somewhat weak/outdated: small (~800k parameter) e3nn models and a 2021-era Graphormer are used for QM9/QM7b/ModelNet40 rather than modern state-of-the-art architectures, so the augmentation-comparison conclusions may not transfer to stronger models.

Some experimental presentation is uneven: the catastrophic FT results (e.g., 7.86% on ModelNet40 transformer) dominate Table 1 and are of limited scientific interest; conversational phrasing ('secretly quite aligned', 'Perhaps the most mysterious takeaway') slightly overstates how surprising the findings are.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: the paper identifies an implicit assumption (p_X ≈ p(gx)) underlying most theoretical and practical work on equivariance and data augmentation, and provides the first practical tool to quantify when it fails.

The proposed classifier two-sample metric m(p_X) is simple, interpretable (bounded accuracy in [1/2, 1]), architecture-flexible compared to kernel-based MMD tests (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy, 2023), and is validated via sanity checks (rotation fraction sweeps on MNIST, MD17; rotated/canonicalized controls in Figure 5), ablations over architecture size, learning rate, and dataset size, and an extension to p-values.

The empirical finding that widely used benchmarks (QM9, QM7b, ModelNet40, MD17, OC20, and even an LLM materials dataset) are heavily canonicalized is surprising and practically useful for the equivariant-ML community; the diagnostic probing of the unknown CORINA canonicalization via classifier decision boundaries is a nice touch.

The theoretical section is technically solid and complements prior work: Theorem 1 extends Elesedy & Zaidi (2021) to non-invariant p_X, shows test-time symmetrization can be arbitrarily harmful (permutation example A.6), and Theorem 2 (with deterministic-equivalent derivations using random matrix theory) establishes when data augmentation hurts in the over-parameterized regime. The appendix observation that gradient descent on equivariant networks is invariant to per-datapoint transformations (A.1) formalizes the intuition that equivariant methods discard distributional asymmetry.

The task-dependent metric t(p_X,Y) and the locality experiments (local QM9, local ModelNet40) go beyond a single number and offer a plausible explanation for the otherwise puzzling discrepancy (ModelNet40 vs. QM9) between symmetry bias and augmentation benefit; the dipole-canonicalization experiment on QM7b cleanly demonstrates a case where non-equivariant training beats equivariant methods.

Broad experimental coverage across domains (vision, 3D shape, molecular ML, catalysis, LLMs) with reported seeds/standard deviations, training details, and a reproducibility statement with public code.
weaknesses: The main metric m(p_X) inherits the usual caveats of classifier two-sample tests: its value depends on classifier capacity, optimization, and sample size, particularly for infinite groups (SO(3)) where no finite upper bound exists. The paper discusses this (Section B, ablations) but the resulting metric is only a lower bound and cross-dataset comparisons (e.g., 97.6% for QM9 vs. 92.45% for ModelNet40) are hard to interpret quantitatively.

The connection between m(p_X)/t(p_X,Y) and downstream augmentation benefit is only partially established. The headline counterintuitive case (QM9: highly canonicalized yet augmentation/equivariance helps) is explained only by a locality hypothesis supported by correlational (not causal) evidence, and the authors themselves acknowledge this ('challenging to establish a causal link'). Figure 6's decision flowchart is heuristic with an arbitrary 50% threshold and no predictive validation.

Theory is confined to ridge(less) regression in the NTK regime and a fairly specialized minimal covariance model (superposition coupling modes, strong-correlation limit); Theorem 2's conditions (γ0 − γc/2 < 1/2, etc.) make it unclear how often the harmful regime arises in practice, and no experiments on real datasets directly test the theoretical predictions.

The downstream experiments use non-SOTA models (Graphormer, e3nn with ~800k params) with only 3 seeds, and some effects (e.g., FT catastrophic degradation; augmentation helping in-distribution training) are close to expected; the more informative comparisons have modest effect sizes relative to seed variance in places.

The task-dependent metric t(p_X,Y) depends on the choice of canonicalization network c(·) and shows overfitting concerns for infinite groups (Section C.2.1); the alternative detection variant was found to be unstable (Tables 6-7), which somewhat undermines confidence in the metric's generality.

Several interesting directions are left underdeveloped: selective augmentation (Figure 17) is a small proof-of-concept on MNIST only, OC20 analysis is acknowledged to be dominated by a trivial slab alignment, and periodic crystals are deferred to future work.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-explored question: quantifying distributional symmetry breaking in datasets and its consequences for equivariant learning and data augmentation.

The proposed classifier two-sample test metric m(p_X) is simple, interpretable, and well-motivated as an alternative to kernel-based tests (e.g., Chiu & Bloem-Reddy 2023) that require kernel selection for geometric graph data.

The theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-invariant covariance is technically substantive: Theorem 1 extends Elesedy & Zaidi (2021) to non-invariant data, and Theorem 2 uses deterministic-equivalent techniques from random matrix theory to show data augmentation can be harmful in the over-parameterized regime when invariant and non-invariant features are correlated.

Empirical coverage is broad (MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, an LLM materials dataset) with sanity checks (rotated/canonicalized controls), synthetic validation, architecture/hyperparameter ablations, and interpretability analyses of the trained classifier.
The locality experiments (local QM9, local ModelNet40) are an interesting and somewhat novel angle for explaining why equivariant methods still help on globally canonicalized datasets.
Reproducibility materials are extensive: detailed training/model specs, per-dataset appendices, loss curves, and a public codebase.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty of the core method: the primary contribution is an application of the well-known classifier two-sample test (Lopez-Paz & Oquab, 2017) to the symmetry-breaking question, which had already been studied with related discriminative/statistical tests (Chiu & Bloem-Reddy, 2023; Desai et al., 2022). The increment over this prior work is real but modest.

The link between the metrics and downstream performance of equivariant methods remains largely qualitative. The paper itself concedes that no threshold for m(p_X) or t(p_X,Y) can currently be determined, and Figure 6's decision flowchart is heuristically assembled rather than empirically validated as a predictive rule. The 'counterintuitive' finding that augmentation helps on QM9/QM7b despite high canonicalization is only explained by an unverified locality hypothesis.

The theory-practice connection is weak: the theoretical guarantees concern linear/ridge regression with Gaussian covariates and specific covariance models, while the empirical claims concern deep GNNs/transformers. The paper offers no quantitative bridge (e.g., testing whether the predicted variance/bias regimes correlate with observed augmentation gaps across datasets).

The task-dependent metric t(p_X,Y) depends critically on the choice of (canonicalization) architecture, which the authors themselves flag as sensitive (Tables 6-7); this undermines its reliability as a practical diagnostic. The relationship between m1 and m2 is only established under restrictive loss/optimization assumptions.

Several experimental comparisons are not convincing: the models used are small and far from state-of-the-art, model capacities differ (e.g., 772K equivariant vs 4.7M transformer), and only 3-5 seeds are used. Some findings (e.g., FT performing poorly at 16.9% accuracy) are near-trivial consequences of test-time distribution mismatch.
The headline empirical conclusion is limited: across all benchmarks, augmentation only really hurts on ModelNet40, which constrains the practical significance of the proposed diagnostic framework.

The deterministic-equivalent machinery in Section A.7 is explicitly acknowledged as not novel (closely following Zavatone-Veth, 2024; Patil, 2022; Atanasov et al., 2024a), reducing the technical novelty of the theory contribution.
Reproducibility is incomplete as submitted: the code URL is blank in the manuscript, so the public-artifact claim cannot be verified.

Presentation issues: several figures are illegibly small (Figures 9-11, 25-27), Table 1 mixes datasets/units in a way that is hard to parse, and the narrative jumps between metrics (m, d_class, m1, m2, t) in a way that makes the contribution structure harder to follow than necessary.

strengths: Introduces a practical, interpretable metric m(pX) for quantifying distributional symmetry breaking via a two-sample classifier test, addressing a genuine gap in the equivariant learning literature where the implicit assumption p(x) ≈ p(gx) is rarely checked.

Complementary theoretical analysis of invariant ridge regression under non-symmetric covariance, covering both under-parameterized and over-parameterized regimes, clearly delineating when augmentation/symmetrization helps or hurts; proofs and deterministic-equivalent derivations appear careful and are grounded in recent random matrix theory.

Impressive breadth of empirical validation: MNIST, ModelNet40, QM9, QM7b, rMD17, OC20, and an LLM materials dataset, with sanity checks (rotated/canonicalized controls), per-class analysis, ablations over architectures/hyperparameters, and p-value extensions comparing against MMD-based tests.

The additional task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) and locality experiments (local QM9/ModelNet40) provide mechanistic insight into why equivariant methods still help on canonicalized datasets, and the practical flowchart (Figure 6) gives practitioners actionable guidance.
Extensive appendices, clear reproducibility statement, and public code make the work largely reproducible.
weaknesses: The connection between m(pX)/t(pX,Y) and downstream augmentation performance is only loosely established: ModelNet40 is essentially the single clear case where train-time augmentation hurts, and the paper itself concedes (Section D.1.2) there is no clear trend between the per-class metric and FF/TF accuracy differences; the QM9 task-dependent signal is small, leaving the predictive power of the metrics under-supported.

The two-sample classifier accuracy depends on the classifier's hypothesis class and optimization; while the paper provides learning-theoretic context (Appendix B) and some ablations, the metric's reliability as a 'distance' is not guaranteed, and sensitivity for subtle asymmetries on infinite groups is not fully characterized.

The theory is confined to linear/ridge regression with Gaussian data and specific covariance models; the extrapolation to deep equivariant networks is motivational rather than proven, and the over-parameterized analysis (Theorem 2) applies only to a minimal covariance model in a limited parameter regime.

The task-dependent metric t(pX,Y) requires a choice of canonicalization network c(·), which the paper acknowledges is sensitive (detection variant was 'overly sensitive' and abandoned); robustness concerns remain for the final metric choice.

Some of the headline findings (e.g., pre-aligned ModelNet40, CORINA canonicalization of QM9, aligned OC20 slabs) are arguably expected from known dataset preprocessing, which somewhat tempers the 'surprising' framing, though the systematic quantification is still valuable.
